title: Principles of health promotion, protection and prevention
blurb: Classify prevention as primary, secondary or tertiary, pick the right health promotion approach and empower people's own choices.
question: Mr Mensah, 63, had a heart attack six weeks ago. He attends cardiac rehabilitation, has started a statin and the practice nurse invites him for bowel screening. Which of these is tertiary prevention, and how should the nurse support his choices?

teach.body: The WHO Ottawa Charter (1986) defines health promotion as the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health. In plain English: helping people take charge of their own health, not doing health to them. The NMC Code 3.1 asks nurses to pay special attention to promoting wellbeing and preventing ill health at all life stages, and Code 2.3 to encourage and empower people to share decisions about their care.

teach.caption: Tannahill (1990): health promotion enhances health and reduces risk through overlapping health education, health protection and disease prevention (HealthKnowledge).
Faculty of Public Health HealthKnowledge prevention definitions.

teach.body: A high-risk approach targets individuals with the highest risk, such as an intensive weight programme for people with a very high BMI. A population approach shifts the whole population a little, such as reducing salt in bread. Geoffrey Rose's prevention paradox: a measure that brings large benefits to the population may offer little benefit to each participating individual, because most cases arise from the many people at moderate risk.

Aim
Example
teach.caption: Ewles and Simnett, Promoting Health (as summarised by HealthKnowledge).

teach.h: Empowering choices within illness or disability
teach.body: Proficiency P2.9 asks nurses to support people to make informed choices to manage health challenges and live well within the limits of illness or disability. That means starting from what matters to the person, offering accurate information in a form they can use, making reasonable adjustments, and agreeing realistic goals (for example swimming instead of long walks for someone with arthritic knees). The person decides; the nurse informs, supports and respects an informed choice, even one the nurse would not make.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Mensah at the GP surgery
teach.body: Mr Mensah, 63, is six weeks after a heart attack. His cardiac rehabilitation and statin are tertiary prevention: they reduce the impact and recurrence of established disease. His bowel screening invitation is secondary prevention. His flu vaccine is primary prevention. Practice nurse Lena asks what matters most to him; he wants to walk his granddaughter to school. Together they set a walking goal, and she offers stop smoking support, which he accepts for next month.

teach.text: Screening is SECONDARY prevention, not primary: it finds disease or risk early in people who feel well; it does not stop the disease starting. And treatment after a diagnosis, such as rehabilitation, is TERTIARY. In this framework a statin after a heart attack counts as tertiary, although cardiology guidance calls it 'secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease'; a statin for raised risk in someone with no disease is primary.

items: Health promotion: enabling people to increase control over, and improve, their health (Ottawa 1986).
Primary prevents onset; secondary detects early (screening); tertiary limits impact of established disease.
High-risk approach targets individuals; population approach shifts everyone a little; prevention paradox.
Five approaches: medical, behaviour change, educational, empowerment, social change.
Empower informed choices within the limits of illness or disability; respect the person's decision.

summary: You can now classify interventions as primary, secondary or tertiary prevention, tell the population approach from the high-risk approach and choose a health promotion approach. You can also support people to make informed choices that fit the limits of their illness or disability.

A.q: A school nurse runs an HPV vaccination session for Year 8 pupils. Which level of prevention is this?
A.why: Immunisation stops disease from starting in healthy people, which is primary prevention (HealthKnowledge).

whyNot.1: Secondary prevention detects disease early, for example screening.
whyNot.2: Tertiary prevention reduces the impact of established disease.
whyNot.3: Surveillance monitors disease patterns; it is not a level of prevention for individuals.

A.q: Mrs Hughes, 58, has type 2 diabetes. She attends a podiatry review to check her feet for early ulceration and to prevent complications. Which level of prevention is the foot review?
A.why: She has established diabetes; reviews to prevent complications and limit its impact are tertiary prevention.

whyNot.0: Primary prevention would prevent diabetes developing in the first place.
whyNot.1: Secondary prevention detects disease early in apparently healthy people, such as screening for diabetes.
whyNot.3: This is an individual intervention, not a population-wide approach.

A.q: A nurse helps a patient practise using a new spacer device and checks his technique. Which Ewles and Simnett approach does this best represent?
A.why: The educational approach gives people knowledge and skills to make informed choices, such as learning inhaler technique.

whyNot.0: Social change works on policy and the environment, not individual skills.
whyNot.2: The medical approach is interventions such as immunisation or screening to prevent disease.
whyNot.3: Empowerment lets the person set the agenda; here the nurse is teaching a set skill.

B.q: A regional public health team works with bakeries to reduce the salt in all bread sold. Which approach to prevention is this?
B.why: Lowering salt for everyone shifts the whole population's risk a little: a population approach (Rose; HealthKnowledge).

whyNot.0: A high-risk approach targets individuals with the highest risk.
whyNot.2: Tertiary prevention is for people with established disease.
whyNot.3: Secondary prevention is early detection, such as screening.

B.q: Beryl, 69, has osteoarthritis of both knees. She wants to be more active but finds walking far painful. She enjoys swimming and the pool is on her bus route. What is the most appropriate nursing approach?
options: Advise a daily 30-minute walk to strengthen her knees
Tell her that exercise is unsafe with arthritis
Refer her for knee replacement before any exercise
Agree a swimming goal that she chooses and can manage
B.why: P2.9: support informed choices to live well within the limits of illness or disability. Building on what Beryl enjoys and can do, with a goal she chooses, is empowering and realistic.

whyNot.0: A walking target ignores her pain and her own preference.
whyNot.1: Activity is generally beneficial and this advice is inaccurate and disempowering.
whyNot.2: Surgery is not a prerequisite for activity and is not the nurse's decision.

B.q: Which statement best describes the prevention paradox?
options: Screening finds more disease in people at low risk
High-risk approaches benefit the whole population most
Prevention costs more overall than treating established disease
Population measures help many but each person gains little
B.why: Rose's prevention paradox: a measure bringing large benefits to the community offers little to each participating individual, because most cases come from the large number of people at moderate risk.

whyNot.0: This is not the paradox; screening yield is highest where risk is higher.
whyNot.1: High-risk approaches benefit the targeted individuals; the paradox concerns population measures.
whyNot.2: The paradox is about distribution of benefit, not cost.

C.q: Tariq, 47, has a BMI of 33. At a health check he says, 'I know I should lose weight, but what I really want is to stop getting out of breath playing football with my son.' Which response best reflects an empowerment approach?
options: Give him a leaflet on the health risks of obesity
Set him a target of losing 10% of his weight
Explore what would help him reach his football goal
Refer him straight to a specialist weight management clinic
C.why: The empowerment approach lets the person set the agenda: Tariq's goal is playing football without breathlessness. Working from his goal respects his choices (Ewles and Simnett; Code 2.3).

whyNot.0: A risk leaflet is an educational or behavioural approach set by the professional.
whyNot.1: A target set by the nurse is a behaviour change approach, not empowerment.
whyNot.3: Referral may help later, but doing it without exploring his goals is professional-led.

C.q: Which pairing of intervention and prevention level is correct?
options: Blood pressure check in a well adult: tertiary
C.why: Rehabilitation after a stroke limits the impact of established disease, which is tertiary prevention.

whyNot.2: Checking BP in a well adult to detect hypertension early is secondary prevention.

C.q: Hazel, 71, has COPD and capacity. After full information she decides not to attend pulmonary rehabilitation, saying she prefers to manage at home. What should the nurse do?
options: Respect her informed choice and offer other support
Ask her family to persuade her to attend
Book the rehabilitation anyway in her best interests
Discharge her from the respiratory nurse caseload
C.why: Code 2.5: respect a person's right to accept or refuse care. An informed decision by a person with capacity is respected, and the nurse offers other support so she can live well with COPD (P2.9).

whyNot.1: Pressuring through family undermines her autonomy.
whyNot.2: Best interests applies to people who lack capacity; Hazel has capacity.
whyNot.3: Declining one intervention is not a reason to withdraw all support.

reteach.title: Before, early, after
reteach.question: Think of a disease as a road. Where on that road does each level of prevention act?

blocks.body: BEFORE the road starts (no disease): primary prevention, such as vaccines, smoking cessation and safe environments. EARLY on the road (disease or risk present but no symptoms): secondary prevention, such as screening and blood pressure checks. AFTER the diagnosis: tertiary prevention, such as rehabilitation and preventing complications.

blocks.text: If the person feels well but is being TESTED for hidden disease, that is secondary prevention, even though they are 'healthy'.

explain.body: Stops disease from starting in healthy people: immunisation, smoking cessation, healthy diet, physical activity, safe environments.

options: Breast screening for a woman of 55
Cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack
Stop smoking support for a healthy adult
Insulin for a child with type 1 diabetes
test.why: Helping a healthy adult stop smoking prevents diseases such as lung cancer and heart disease developing: primary prevention.

whyNot.1: Rehabilitation after a cardiac event: tertiary.
whyNot.3: Insulin treats established disease: tertiary or treatment.

explain.body: Detects disease or risk early in apparently healthy people, so treatment is more effective: national screening, blood pressure checks, NHS Health Checks.

test.q: Sunil, 65, has no symptoms and is invited for AAA ultrasound screening. Which level of prevention is this?
test.why: Screening apparently healthy people to detect disease early is secondary prevention.

whyNot.0: Primary prevention would stop an aneurysm forming.
whyNot.3: Quaternary prevention is about avoiding overmedicalisation, not screening.

explain.body: Medical (immunise, screen), behaviour change (change lifestyle), educational (knowledge and skills), empowerment (person sets the agenda), social change (policy and environment).

test.q: A council introduces a ban on smoking in children's playgrounds. Which approach is this?
test.why: Changing laws, policy or the environment is the social change approach.

whyNot.1: Empowerment lets individuals set their own agenda.
whyNot.3: Behaviour change works with individuals to change their lifestyle.

explain.body: Start with what matters to the person; give accurate, accessible information; make reasonable adjustments; agree realistic goals; respect informed decisions (Code 2.3, 2.5; P2.9).

test.q: Which NMC Code clause asks nurses to encourage and empower people to share decisions about their treatment and care?
test.why: NMC Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions about their treatment and care.

whyNot.1: 5.4 concerns sharing information when safety overrides confidentiality.
whyNot.2: 10.1 is about completing records at the time.
whyNot.3: 13.2 is about making a timely referral.
